cases.reason: ["1"] is what a manifest omitting contractVersions resolves to, so this pins the absence-defaults-to-["1"] assertion, not only that agreement is possible.
The largest common major wins, not the first match in either set's order.
"10" sorts before "9" as a string, so numeric-length comparison is required.
A major long enough to lose precision under Number(), so comparison must be on digit strings.
The agreed major does not depend on the declared order of either peer's set.
The mirror ordering of negotiate-order-a, so neither peer's order can be swapped to change the outcome.
Two well-formed sets sharing no member — the plain no-common-version refusal.
An empty local set, paired with negotiate-empty-remote so a one-directional intersection cannot pass both.
An empty remote set, the mirror of negotiate-empty-local.
A leading zero is invalid-version, not no-common-version — validation precedes intersection.
A non-string member must not be coerced before the pattern is checked.
A Unicode digit that looks like an ASCII one must still be refused by an ASCII-only pattern.
A duplicated member reaching the algorithm directly is accepted, not refused — uniqueness is enforced one layer earlier (§4, §5), never re-checked here.
The canonical frame the reference encoder emits.
Insignificant whitespace does not change the parse.
Member order is insignificant in JSON.
Unknown members are ignored, not rejected.
Not syntactically JSON, refused before any member is inspected.
Valid JSON but not an object.
Valid JSON, array-shaped, but not an object — the frame itself, not a value inside it.
A well-formed envelope for a different message — the discriminator makes a frame a hello.
The discriminator is present but contractVersions never arrives.

missing-versions covers both an absent field and a present non-array — a binding answering invalid-version or not-object here would still pass every other case, which is exactly why this one is needed.
contractVersions is present but declares nothing.
The same major declared twice must be refused, not collapsed into a set.
A Unicode digit escaped inside the frame string must still be refused as invalid-version.
A leading zero in the announced set exercises the frame parser's own validation, distinct from the negotiate-kind case of the same shape.
The running peer announces exactly what its manifest declared.
The same majors in a different order still match, because comparison is on sets.
An absent manifest declaration exercises the default of ["1"].
A superset is the interesting failure the confirm step exists to catch.
The absent-manifest default is not a license for the running peer to announce more.
A non-array manifest declaration reaches the comparison rather than being dropped, and case.schema.json's own manifest property promises exactly this is refused.
